videos.title: Inside Theranos with ex-Employee Tyler Shultz
videos.description:
With Theranos and Elizabeth Holmes back in the conversation, we’re revisiting one of the most remarkable firsthand accounts of what actually happened inside the company.

Tyler Shultz joined Theranos fresh out of Stanford as a true believer in its mission. His grandfather, former Secretary of State George Shultz, sat on the company’s board, and Elizabeth Holmes had become a mentor and even a presence at family gatherings. But once Tyler began working directly with Theranos’s technology, he discovered that the reality inside the lab looked very different from what the company was telling the world.

On The Social Radars, Tyler sat down with Jessica Livingston and Carolynn Levy to tell the full story of how he went from employee to whistleblower: the failed blood tests and red flags he uncovered, the culture of fear that kept employees silent, his attempts to raise concerns internally and with regulators, and the extraordinary legal pressure he faced after speaking to The Wall Street Journal.

This episode was originally recorded on December 4, 2024.

videos.title: Rokib Al Dhin Raadh - When the Update Is Not a Gradient
videos.description:
​Every standard convergence proof for gradient descent assumes that each update is a gradient. Self-repairing training violates that assumption by design, and it still converges. This session shows why, and exactly where the proof stops.

Zero out a converged convolutional layer at epoch 100. A parameter-matched baseline remains at chance on every seed (10.0% ± 0.0%). A self-repairing network recovers to 80.3% ± 1.6% through 85 bounded, logged corrections. Those corrections are state-dependent, diagnostic-triggered and discontinuous; they are the gradient of no objective. Why the trajectory does not diverge is a genuinely mathematical question.

We model training as a switched dynamical system (contractive gradient flow, bounded disturbance, isolated resets) and derive a practical input-to-state stability bound under local L-smoothness and α-strong convexity:

limsup ‖θₜ − θ*‖ ≤ γ = 2βM/α + ε_max/(ηα)

The bound is non-vacuous only if correction magnitude decays, so the stability claim becomes a falsifiable prediction. Within a 383-run evaluation, it holds: correction magnitude falls by 83–93%.

The most instructive part is the gap between theory and observation. The per-step contraction the proof relies on holds on only 31.6% of steps, yet the run converges. The offset term never vanishes, so the result is practical rather than strict ISS. Forward invariance of the neighbourhood remains unproven.

We close on the open problems: deriving ε(t) from first principles, relaxing strong convexity to Polyak–Łojasiewicz, and dwell-time conditions for discrete reinitializations. Attendees are invited to challenge the bound directly.
preprint: https://zenodo.org/records/21730363

​Bio:
Rokib Al Dhin Raadh is an 18y old researcher working on the stability and auditability of neural network training dynamics, without institutional affiliation. He is the sole author of ORMAS, an architecture that localizes, repairs and logs its own component-level failures during training, validated across 383 controlled experiments on four architectures. His input-to-state stability analysis of self-repairing training was accepted at DeepMath 2026 (Conference on the Mathematical Theory of Deep Neural Networks) after double-blind review. He serves as a reviewer for the NeurIPS 2026 Trustworthy AI for Good workshop and is a member of the Cohere Labs Open Science Community. He is the founder of Oxiedo.

This session is brought to you by the Cohere Labs Open Science Community -  a space where 
ML researchers, engineers, linguists, social scientists, and lifelong learners connect and collaborate with each other. We'd like to extend a special thank you to Katrina Lawrence and Neel Ghoshal,  Leads of our ML Math group for their dedication in organizing this event. 

If you’re interested in sharing your work, we welcome you to join us! Simply fill out the form at https://forms.gle/ALND9i6KouEEpCnz6 to express your interest in becoming a speaker.

videos.title: How Anthropic ships the #1 LLM in the World — with Katelyn Lesse and Angela Jiang
videos.description:
An agent’s sandbox can die without taking the whole agent with it. That’s the idea behind “the brain and the hands,” Anthropic’s architecture for Claude Managed Agents.

Now that the dust has settled on Opus 5.5, it is universally agreed to be the best model in the world. In this conversation with Katelyn Lesse and Angela Jiang, Anthropic’s Heads of Engineering and of Product, goes inside the systems that turn model capabilities into products developers can use.

We cover:

- Why Anthropic separated the agent harness, session state and execution environment.
- Letting agents use credentials without putting those credentials inside their sandboxes.
- Rebuilding the Messages API from Python to Rust with Claude—and verifying the rewrite with shadow traffic.
- Preventing model distillation while preserving the developer experience.
- Memory, “dreaming,” agent evaluations and the work still left for human engineers.
- How Anthropic’s own teams use Claude while keeping responsibility for their code and writing.

The episode opens with swyx’s look at Anthropic’s S-1: revenue per employee, compute efficiency, and the improvement and investment loops behind the business.

**Related links**

- [Claude Opus 5.5](https://www.anthropic.com/claude-opus-5-5) — Performance, pricing and safeguards.
- [The brain and the hands](https://www.anthropic.com/research/managed-agents) — The Managed Agents architecture.
- [How Anthropic contains Claude](https://www.anthropic.com/research/how-we-contain-claude) — Isolation, credentials and network controls.
- [Harnesses for long-running agents](https://www.anthropic.com/research/effective-harnesses-for-long-running-agents) — Maintaining progress across context windows.

videos.title: Turning Stranded Energy Into Intelligence: Crusoe CEO Chase Lochmiller
videos.description:
Chase Lochmiller runs one of the most operationally complex companies in AI: Crusoe builds power plants, manufactures electrical equipment, operates gigawatt-scale data centers, and runs a managed AI cloud on top, all under one roof. He just closed a round at a $31 billion valuation, and he got there by selling off the Bitcoin mining business that was paying the bills.

Chase explains why Crusoe is modeled on Exxon, not a cloud provider, and why he partners with companies that look like competitors. He makes the case that a company that outgrows the person who got it there is the rule, not the exception, and that CEOs almost always fire too slowly. He also talks candidly about hiring a coach, working hard to become a polished speaker when it didn’t come naturally, and why the data center industry’s biggest problem is a marketing problem.

I meet with a group of Sequoia founder CEOs between 20 and 2,000 employees, and one of them told me his business is becoming dizzyingly complex beneath him. Chase has the clearest answer I’ve heard for how to hold that in your head. 

And yes, we talk about summiting Everest.

videos.title: Inside the Robot Data Factory: Mecka's Josh Gao on Sensorizing Humans to Train Robots
videos.description:
Robotics never got the internet's gift of free training data, so someone has to manufacture it. Josh Gao, founder and CEO of Mecka AI, runs one of the largest robot data factories, and he explains what that actually involves: custom baseball caps and tactile gloves because nothing off the shelf captures force, 100-gigabit upload lines to move hundreds of petabytes, and custom quality gates. Josh lays out the training recipe the industry is converging on (roughly a million hours of egocentric human data, tens of thousands of hours of robot data, and a few hours of in-domain teleop ) and why tactile and simulation data still have to enter the "data pot of soup." He argues the field is still orders of magnitude behind Tesla's FSD, which spent a decade on two degrees of freedom while a robot hand has dozens. His take: there won't be a single GPT-3 moment for robotics, but a steady unlock of commercial tasks, starting with constrained industrial work and ending, he hopes, with robots mining asteroids.

Hosted by Sonya Huang, Sequoia Capital

videos.title: Confronting Our AI Future: Closing Keynote "Discovery Loop" with Jeff Dean and Fei-Fei Li
videos.description:
This closing fireside chat brings together two of the field's most consequential builders — Jeff Dean, whose work at Google has helped define the modern AI stack, and Fei-Fei Li, whose case for human-centered AI has shaped how the field thinks about who this technology should actually serve. Coming at the end of a day spent grappling with AI's risks and unresolved questions, the conversation turns to where the two of them agree, where they don't, and what they think the choices ahead really come down to.

*Speakers:* 

- Fei-Fei Li: Inaugural Sequoia Professor in the Computer Science Department at Stanford University, and a Founding Director of HAI. She served as the Director of Stanford’s AI Lab from 2013 to 2018. Li has served as a Vice President at Google and Chief Scientist of AI/ML at Google Cloud (2017-2018), board member or advisor in various public or private companies and is currently a Co-founder/CEO of World Labs, an AI company focusing on Spatial Intelligence and generative AI. 

- Jeff Dean: Computer scientist and software engineer. He is best known for his work at Google, which he joined in 1999. He led Google AI from 2018 to 2023 and was Google's chief scientist from 2023 to 2026. Dean co-founded the AI research start-up Discovery Loop in 2026.

He also introduces a self-report tool that agents can call to flag what went wrong while they run, and shares that Engine has scanned over 70 million traces and detected over 21,000 issues.
